At 4:17 every morning, the clock above Mara’s station stopped, and the city appeared beyond the river. It arrived without footsteps: a silver skyline rising from the fog, its towers carved with windows that held the amber light of another century. By 4:18, it was gone, leaving wet asphalt, dark water, and the smell of coffee from somewhere no longer existed. Mara was the only person who had seen it, but the next night she began hearing a telephone ring beneath the river. She kept her recorder running, afraid to miss whatever the city might say for one whole night.

The call came again on the third night, soft and patient, each ring rising through the concrete floor. She followed a maintenance ladder down to the riverbank, carrying a lantern and her father’s old brass key. Between two pilings, she found a door that hadn’t been there before, its paint the deep green of bottle glass. When she turned the key, a telephone hung in the fog, ringing beside a road leading into empty darkness. No buildings. No stars. Only a distant clock gathering courage to strike. Its echo traveled through water, across streets, and into her waiting hand slowly.

She lifted the receiver. Instead of a voice, static crackled, then a girl spoke clearly: “Mara, don’t cross at the fourth bell.” The girl said the city was Bellweather, erased from every map after a flood in 1893. Mara knew the name. Her grandfather Elias had guarded the eastern station, and his journals described strangers arriving with clocks stopped at 4:17. “They are reminders,” he had written, “that waiting is not the same as being lost.” Mara searched his last page, where fresh ink shone: “When the river rings, let your answer be footsteps.” “Bring nothing, and trust no mirror.”

At 4:16 the next morning, Mara stood before the green door, dressed in a red coat against the November rain. The river sounded with invisible bells, each note loosening the distance between moments. Her grandfather’s key warmed in her palm; the telephone answered with one sharp, eager click. Then the road opened, and Mara crossed into Bellweather. Fog curled around her ankles, but the city was waiting, every lamp burning and every shop door unlatched. Windows gleamed like dark eyes, watching her pass. Above the rooftops, the great clock waited. And somewhere nearby, a girl began to sing very softly.

The singer stood beneath an awning, perhaps seventeen, perhaps forty; time had polished uncertainty from her face. She wore blue and held Mara’s recorder like a captured bird. “You shouldn’t have come,” she said, smiling as though they had waited years. Mara looked around. The silent streets belonged to no era, yet every detail felt painfully familiar. “The bakery smells tomorrow,” the girl continued, guiding Mara toward a clockmaker’s shop. “Don’t enter the tower unless you understand what it asks.” “Some prisoners guard other prisons, and every locked door becomes a choice. But time is the least of our walls.”

Inside the shop, clocks crowded every surface: pocket watches, alarms, watches shaped like flowers, and one large moon-faced clock ticking backward. The girl touched its glass. “Bellweather doesn’t disappear when the flood comes. It withdraws into the minutes it borrows.” From an inner room came the scrape of a chair, followed by a man in a black coat. He looked at Mara without surprise. “Vale,” he said. “Your great-great-grandfather left his watch here. He said someone would return for it.” “We keep unfinished things. The city is made of departures that never learned how to end.” “A prison?” Mara asked.

Up a spiral staircase, the tower’s keeper waited beside a radio, its green light blinking like a steady heart. He was the black-coated man, though Mara could not remember him wearing the coat downstairs. The keeper tuned static until her recorder spoke in the girl’s voice: “Fourth bell. River gate. One traveler.” He explained that Bellweather existed inside a single stolen minute, repeating itself while everyone else continued toward morning. “Every seventeen years, the river permits a visitor. The city may keep them, or release them, but it always demands a keeper in return.” “Do you then volunteer?” Mara asked.

The keeper placed an old pocket watch in Mara’s hand. Its hands circled the moment of her first memory. “Your watch will hold the city, but only your choice can open the gate.” Mara imagined her life continuing: cold mornings, unanswered applications, and a rented room overlooking an unremarkable road. She imagined another life, too: Bellweather’s crowded streets, the girl’s laughter, mornings that smelled of bread instead of disappointment. The fourth bell began to tremble through the tower. “If I stay, someone else must cross in seventeen years. If I go, this city will finally end.” Mara watched him silently.

The keeper pressed a key into her palm. “The river returns what it borrows, but only after the clock remembers how to move.” Mara ran down, faster than she had climbed, while bells shattered the windows behind her. At the green door, the blue-dressed girl waited with tears shining on both cheeks. “Will you remember us?” she asked. “I have kept your names, the smell of coffee, and every echo of your city’s bells.” “I will carry Bellweather in my pocket, beside my grandfather’s watch, until my hands forget how to tremble.” “Promise,” the girl whispered, “you’ll return.”

Mara stepped through. The rain struck her coat, and the river rang its final, fading bell. Bellweather vanished behind her, taking the clocktower, the blue-dressed girl, and all those borrowed tomorrows. She reached the station at dawn, clutching her recorder and the black-coated man’s pocket watch. The watch showed an impossible time: 4:17, every hour, every day. Yet beneath the static, she could still hear the distant tower chiming, steady and clear. She wrote a note to her grandfather: “You were right. Waiting is not the same as being lost.” That night, she did not dream. She listened to bells.
